questions_and_answers.question_text: What does xīn mean when used as an adverb?
Name the three comparison patterns and their purposes.
What kind of verb is the comparison made with in all three patterns?
How do you indicate HOW MUCH more one thing is than another?
Which two adverbs are used to compare more than two things?
Write the Chinese for "I am two years older than she is."
Write the Chinese for "Going by train is not as fast as going by plane."

answers.answer_text: Zuò huǒchē méiyou zuò fēijī nàme kuài.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Should you use the negative of the bǐ pattern to say "less"?
Write the Chinese for "This is much better looking than that!"
Name three kinds of state verb that may be used in a comparison.

answers.answer_text: Adjectival verbs (hǎo), auxiliary verbs (huì), and verbs describing mental attitudes (zhīdao, xǐhuan, ài).

Notes on No. 3

Xīn kāide: The adjectival verb xīn, "new," means "newly," "recently" when used as an adverb.

Gèng, "more," "even more," "still more"

Zài lǐngshìguǎn gōngzuòde rén    More people work at the consulates
bǐ dàshǐguǎn gèng duō.           than at the embassy.
Lǜ píngguǒ hěn guì, hóng         Green apples are expensive; red
píngguǒ gèng guì.                apples are even more expensive.

AN OVERVIEW OF COMPARISON: You have now learned several ways to compare things. Each pattern has a standard purpose:

(MORE)   ...bǐ...(STATE VERB)
(LESS)   ...méiyou...nàme (STATE VERB)
(EQUAL)  ...gēn...yíyàng (STATE VERB)

A simple adjectival verb may also be used to make a comparison:

Zhèi liǎngběn, něiběn guì?       Which of these two books is more
                                 expensive?

For each of the three patterns above (MORE--LESS--EQUAL), the comparison is made with a STATE verb. State verbs include adjectival verbs (hǎo, "to be good"), auxiliary verbs (huì, "to know how to," "can"), and verbs describing mental attitudes or situations (zhīdao, "to know"; xǐhuan, "to like"; ài, "to love").

Tā bǐ wǒ ài chī Zhōngguo fàn.    He loves to eat Chinese food more
                                 than I.
Zhèijiàn shìqing, nǐ bǐ tā       You know more about this than he does.
zhīdao.
Tā méiyou wǒ zhème xǐhuan        He doesn't like to see movies as
kàn diànyǐng.                    much as I do.

The things being compared may also be expanded. Whole sentences may be placed in the slots for things compared:

Zuò huǒchē méiyou zuò fēijī      Going by train is not as fast as
nàme kuài.                       going by plane.

Although the prepositional verb bǐ is used to say that one thing is "more" than another, do not use the negative of this pattern to say that something is "less."

This pattern may also be expanded to indicate just HOW MUCH more one thing is than another. (Place the amount after the verb in a sentence.)

Zhèiběn bǐ nèiběn guì sānkuài    This book is three dollars more
qián.                            expensive than that one.
Wǒ bǐ ta dà liǎngsuì.            I am two years older than she is.

Another way to indicate how much more is to add -de duō, "a lot," to an adjectival verb.

Zhèige bǐ nèige hǎokànde duō!    This is much better looking than that!

Use the pattern ...méiyou...nàme + state verb to say that one thing is less than another.

The affirmative pattern ...yǒu...nàme + state verb is ambiguous: it says that one item is AT LEAST AS expensive as another item. This pattern is not as common as ...méiyou...nàme + state verb.

The adverbs gèng, "even more," and zuì, "most," are easily used to compare more than two things. (Place these adverbs before the verb in a sentence.)

Zhèi liǎngběn hěn guì, kěshi     These two books are very expensive,
nèiběn gèng guì.                 but that one is even more expensive.
Zhèi sānběn shū, něiběn guì?     Of these three books, which is the
                                 (most) expensive one?
Zhèiběn zuì guì.                 This one is the most expensive.
